label: Person
name: Adolfo Alejandro Nouel
summary:
Adolfo Alejandro Nouel (1862–1937) was a Dominican Catholic archbishop who served as Archbishop of Santo Domingo and—uniquely among Catholic clergy in the Americas—served briefly as President of the Dominican Republic in 1912–1913. Born in Santo Domingo into a distinguished Dominican family, he was educated in Rome and ordained a priest before rising to the archbishopric.

In 1912, as the Dominican Republic descended into political crisis with multiple factions contesting the presidency, the major parties agreed that only a universally respected figure outside politics could serve as a transitional president. Nouel was unanimously elected by the Dominican Congress in November 1912 and served as president until April 1913, when he resigned, exhausted by the intractable political divisions. He was the only Latin American Catholic bishop to serve as head of state in the twentieth century outside of the Vatican context.

His presidential term was marked by diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis without external intervention, particularly from the United States, which was then asserting increasing influence over Caribbean affairs. After resigning, he returned to his ecclesiastical duties and continued as archbishop until 1935. His brief but remarkable political career illustrates the extraordinary authority that Catholic archbishops commanded in early twentieth-century Latin American societies, where Church and state were intimately intertwined.
